attributes.article_four_hazard:
THE FOURTH ARTICLE (Hazard), added RR 167. 'Water rising or standing within the bounds is a hazard to the crossings and is held in trust by the Wardenry. Where such water is found, a Warden of the Third Rank or above, standing upon the ground and speaking before two witnesses, may declare the ground about it a hazard, and set a seal upon it, and hold it against all comers until the hazard is surveyed and lifted. The Wardenry shall pay the finder the worth of the ground at the last assessed price of salt.

Provided always, that the seal be entered upon the roll at Bell Harrow within forty days of the speaking of it. A seal not so entered is no seal from the day it was set; the ground is free of it; and the same ground shall not be declared again for the space of a year.

Provided also, that the seal lie upon the ground and the water and upon nothing else. It shall not reach to survey, level, note, log nor instrument, nor to the person carrying the same, nor compel the showing of them. Papers are the goods of him that holds them, and go off the ground in his hand.

Provided lastly, that where the master of a lawful crossing stands upon sealed ground, holding his tile whole, he may require of the Warden, before the same two witnesses, that the survey be begun before the turn of the season next following; and the Warden shall enter the requirement upon the roll beside the seal, and the Wardenry shall appoint the surveyor and bear the cost of him. A requirement so made is not undone by the after-breaking of the tile. But a tile broken before the speaking of it is no licence, and he that holds no licence may require nothing. And if the season turn and no survey be begun, the seal is lifted of itself, and the ground is free, and the Wardenry shall not declare the same ground again upon the same water.'
attributes.article_one_bounds: THE FIRST ARTICLE (Bounds). 'The bounds of the Meniscus are all ground lying below the old shoreline and bearing salt to the depth of a man's arm. Within the bounds the Wardenry answers for the crossings. Beyond them it answers for nothing.'
attributes.article_three_water: THE THIRD ARTICLE (Water). 'Every licensed crossing shall carry water to the measure of two gallons the head the day, and shall answer for it at the far rim. Every well within the bounds is the Wardenry's to open, to close and to ration.'
attributes.article_two_licence: THE SECOND ARTICLE (Licence), original to RR 1 — quoted here entire, revocation clause and all. 'No wagon, beast or person shall pass the bounds unlicensed. A licence is a fired tile, stamped to a roll number, a route and a season, carried by the master of the crossing and surrendered at the far rim. A broken tile is no licence. A Warden of the Third Rank or above may revoke a licence upon the road, by breaking the tile in the holder's hand and in his sight, speaking the cause before he breaks it and before one witness that can be named; and the halves shall be kept and carried back to the roll at Bell Harrow, and the cause entered there beside the roll number. A Warden below the Third Rank may take up a tile and report it, and may not break it. The master may sue the cause at the rim and be paid his loss if the cause fail; but the tile once broken is not mended, and the crossing does not pass.'
attributes.date: RR 1 — the year the calendar starts; two centuries before the present
attributes.how_to_invoke_it_correctly: Warden of Third Rank or above, physically on the ground, says it aloud, names two witnesses, sets the seal. Forty days to the Bell Harrow roll or the seal is no seal. Site held, papers untouched, compensation owed. Then the clock: any master of a lawful crossing standing on that ground with an unbroken tile can require the survey inside a season, and the Warden has to enter the requirement on the roll beside her own seal. That is the whole mechanism, and the order of events is the chapter: seal, then requirement, and whichever of the tile and the sentence comes first decides the book. Nothing more is needed and nothing less will do.
attributes.limits: All five of these are in the text of the Articles themselves — the four provisos of the Fourth and the revocation clause of the Second — not gloss laid over them. Iseul Fane can recite them from memory, and does. (1) BOUNDS ONLY — it reaches water inside the Meniscus and nowhere else; water at the rim is beyond it entirely. (2) FORTY DAYS — a seal not entered on the Bell Harrow roll within forty days is no seal from the day it was set, and the same ground cannot be re-declared for a year. Bell Harrow is 385 miles and twenty days from the centre, so the forty days is a real ride, not a formality. (3) GROUND, NOT PAPER — it seizes ground and water and has no reach whatever over surveys, levels, notes, logs, instruments or the people carrying them, and cannot compel their showing. The packet cannot be taken under this Article. (4) COMPENSATION — the finder is owed the worth of the ground at the last assessed salt price, payable at Bell Harrow. Refusing to pay does not void the seal, but it stands as a debt on the Wardenry's roll and can be sued at the rim. (5) THE SEASON CLOCK — the master of a lawful crossing, standing on sealed ground with his tile whole, may require the survey be begun before the turn of the next season; the Warden must enter the requirement on the roll beside the seal, and if the season turns unsurveyed the seal lifts of itself and that ground can never be sealed again over that water. The Wardenry still appoints the surveyor. It is the only limit in the Article with teeth, and it has exactly one weakness: it rides on a fired tile the size of a palm.
attributes.sealed_at: Bell Harrow, by eleven route-keepers and the councils of two rim-cities
attributes.structure: four articles. The first three are original to RR 1; the Fourth was added in RR 167 after the Brackening at Sixty Wells.
attributes.the_abuse: 'Until the hazard is surveyed and lifted' has no outer bound, and the Wardenry appoints its own surveyor. The Ferrant seal of RR 189 is still in force and its survey has never been begun. Unless a licence-holder forces the season clock, a hazard declaration is permanent. And the cheapest answer to a licence-holder is the Second Article: break the tile in his hand before the requirement is spoken, and there is no licence-holder on the ground to speak it. The two Articles were sealed a hundred and sixty-six years apart and nobody has ever had to read them against each other, because until now no tile has ever been standing on sealed ground with a reason to.
attributes.the_argument_available:
The Article's own words are the argument. It reaches "water rising or standing within the bounds". The centre's water does neither: it lies between nine and fourteen feet under the crust, in wet gravel over the grey clay, and it had to be augered up in a bucket before anybody could look at it. A rim advocate can argue in good faith that a lens nine feet down is not water rising and not water standing — that the Third Article gave the Wardenry every well within the bounds, that the Fourth extended that to water a man can see, and that a thing you must dig for is neither. The Wardenry's answer is short and not stupid: nine feet is a spade and an afternoon, the first man who digs it will have water standing in a hole by evening, and the Article was written against the day after that. No rim court has ever ruled on the point. The case has never been brought, because until this survey there was nothing under the bounds worth bringing it about.

What this is not is an argument about why nobody found it sooner. Nothing was hidden. Wet ground on the plain reads as brine: rotten crust is a standing hazard of the Meniscus, a soft patch with brine sitting under a thin lid, and the first thing a driver learns in his first season is to steer around it and put neither wheel nor spade in it. Two centuries of caravans walked past the centre's brown ground and correctly identified it as the thing that kills you. It never took a survey to find wet ground out there. It took a College-sealed water-glass, floated against a known brine, to say in about a minute that this wet ground was fresh. One instrument, one seal, one reading: that is the whole distance between a hazard everyone sensibly avoided and a find that ends the Road.
attributes.the_untested_question: The Article says the Wardenry shall pay 'the finder'. It has never been invoked where the finder was himself a Warden. If Denet Rasca is the finder, the Wardenry owes itself, and he has standing inside the institution that no outsider has ever had. Nobody at Bell Harrow knows what that means, including the people who will invoke it.
attributes.what_it_permits: Sealing the ground about the water and holding it against all comers — including the finder — for as long as the hazard is 'under survey'. In practice: post wardens, cap or fence the water, and exclude everyone from the site.
attributes.who_may_invoke_the_fourth: A Warden of the Third Rank or above, in person. The declaration must be spoken aloud on the ground itself, before two witnesses who can be named, and entered on the roll at Bell Harrow within forty days. It cannot be declared by letter, by proxy, or from the rim — somebody of rank has to physically stand on the site, which at the centre means three hundred and eighty-five miles and twenty laden days, or fifteen in a forced run, to say one sentence. The forty days to the roll then has to be ridden back over the same ground.

name: The Sealing of the Roadwarden Statute
summary: Eleven route-keepers and two rim-city councils met at Bell Harrow and wrote down what had until then been custom: who may cross, who carries water, and who answers when a crossing is lost. The document they sealed created the Wardenry in the act of describing it, and the calendar has been counted from it ever since. It has been amended exactly once, in RR 167, and that amendment is the one that matters now.
